{{Short description|Math concept}}
{{Technical|introduction|date=December 2025}}
In mathematics, especially [[algebraic topology]], an '''absolute neighborhood retract''' (or '''ANR''') is a "nice"{{Weasel inline|date=May 2026}} [[topological space]] that is considered in [[homotopy theory]]; more specifically, in the theory of [[Retraction (topology)|retracts]].{{efn|A retraction is a continuous mapping from a topological space into a subspace that preserves the position of all points in that subspace.<ref>Borsuk (1931)</ref>}}

For a more general introduction to ANRs, see also [[Retraction (topology)#Absolute neighborhood retract (ANR)]]. This article focuses more on results on ANRs.

== Definitions ==
Given a class <math>\mathfrak c</math> of topological spaces, an '''absolute retract''' for <math>\mathfrak c</math> is a topological space <math>X</math> in <math>\mathfrak c</math> such that for each closed embedding <math>X \hookrightarrow Y</math> into a space <math>Y</math> in <math>\mathfrak c</math>, <math>X</math> (that is, the image of <math>X</math>) is a retract of <math>Y</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Mardešić|1999|page=242}}</ref>

An '''absolute neighborhood retract''' or '''ANR''' for <math>\mathfrak c</math> is a topological space <math>X</math> in <math>\mathfrak c</math> such that for each closed embedding <math>X \hookrightarrow Y</math> into a space <math>Y</math> in <math>\mathfrak c</math>, <math>X</math> is a retract of a neighborhood in <math>Y</math>. In literature, it is the most common to take <math>\mathfrak c</math> to be the class of [[metric space]]s or separable metric spaces. The notion of ANRs is due to Borsuk.<ref>Karol Borsuk, Über eine Klasse von lokal zusammenhängenden Räumen, Fund. Math 19 (1932) 220-242</ref>

A closely related notion is that of an '''absolute extensor'''; namely, an '''absolute extensor''' is a topological space <math>X</math> such that for each <math>Y</math> in <math>\mathfrak c</math> and a closed subset <math>A \subset Y</math>, each continuous map <math>A \to X</math> extends to <math>Y \to X</math>. An '''absolute neighborhood extensor''' is defined similarly by requiring the existence of an extension only to a neighborhood of <math>A</math>.

== Results ==
The next theorem characterizes an ANR in terms of the extension property.

{{math_theorem|math_statement=<ref>{{harvnb|Dugundji|1951|loc=Theorem 7.1.}}</ref> The following are equivalent for a metric space <math>Y</math>:
# <math>Y</math> is an ANR for metric spaces.
# There is an embedding <math>Y \hookrightarrow E</math> into a normed linear space such that <math>Y</math> is a retract of a neighborhood in the convex hull of the image of <math>Y</math>.
# For each metric space <math>X</math> and closed subset <math>A \subset X</math>, each <math>A \to Y</math> extends to a neighborhood of <math>A</math>; in short, <math>Y</math> is an absolute neighborhood extensor.}}

This is a consequence of [[Dugundji's extension theorem]] and the [[Eilenberg–Wojdysławski theorem]]. Indeed, the latter theorem says every metric space embeds into a normed space as a closed subset of the convex hull of the image. This gives <math>1 \Rightarrow 2</math>. Assuming <math>Y \subset U \subset K = </math> the convex hull of <math>Y</math> and a retraction <math>r : U \to Y</math> exists, by Dugundji's extension theorem, each <math>A \to Y \subset K</math> extends to <math>g : X \to K</math>. Then <math>g^{-1}(U) \overset{g}\to U \overset{r}\to Y</math> is a required extension. Finally, <math>3 \Rightarrow 1</math> holds by taking <math>A = Y</math>. <math>\square</math>

There is also the notion of a '''local ANR''', a metric space in which each point has a neighborhood that is an ANR. But as it turns out, the two notions ANR and local ANR coincide.<ref>{{harvnb|Hanner|1951|loc=Theorem 3.2.}}</ref> In particular, a topological manifold is an ANR (even strongly it is a [[Euclidean neighborhood retract]].)

There is also the following type of the approximation theorem

{{math_theorem|math_statement=<ref>{{harvnb|Hanner|1951|loc=Theorem 4.1.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Dugundji|1951|loc=Lemma 7.2.}}</ref> Let <math>Y</math> be an ANR and <math>\alpha</math> an open cover of <math>Y</math>. Then there exists a refinement <math>\beta</math> of <math>\alpha</math> with the property: if two maps <math>f, g : X \to Y</math> from a separable metric space are <math>\beta</math>-near in the sense <math>f^{-1}(U) \cap g^{-1}(U), U \in \beta</math> is an open cover of <math>Y</math>, then there is an <math>\alpha</math>-homotopy <math>h_t</math> between them; i.e., <math>h_0, h_1 = f, g</math> and for each <math>x</math> in <math>X</math>, <math>h_I(x) \subset </math> some open set in <math>\alpha</math>. Moreover, <math>\beta</math> has the property: if a priori a <math>\beta</math>-homotopy <math>f|A \sim g|A</math> is given for some closed subset <math>A</math>, then the above homotopy can be taken to be an extension of that.

Conversely,<ref>{{harvnb|Hanner|1951|loc=Theorem 4.2.}}</ref> a separable metric space <math>Y</math> is an ANR if there exists an open cover <math>\alpha</math> of <math>Y</math> with the property: for a pair of <math>\alpha</math>-near maps <math>f, g: X \to Y</math>, each <math>\alpha</math>-homotopy <math>f|A \sim g|A</math> extends to a homotopy <math>f \sim g</math>.}}

The theorem in particular implies that an ANR is locally contractible in the geometric topology sense; i.e., given a neighborhood <math>V</math> of a point, the natural inclusion from some smaller neighborhood of the same point <math>V \hookrightarrow U</math> is nullhomotopic. On the other hand, Borsuk has given an example of a locally contractible space that is not an ANR.<ref>Borsuk, Karol. "Sur un espace compact localement contractile qui n'est pas un rétracte absolu de voisinage." Fundamenta Mathematicae 35 (1948): 175-180.</ref> What we can say is: if <math>X</math> is a locally contractible separable metric space and the [[homotopy extension theorem]] holds for it, then <math>X</math> is an ANR.<ref>{{harvnb|Hanner|1951|loc=Theorem 5.3.}}</ref>

An ''n''-[[covering dimension|dimensional]] metric space  is an ANR if and only if it is [[locally connected up to dimension]] ''n'' in the sense of Lefschetz.<ref>The separable case is due to {{cite journal |last1=Kuratowski |first1=Casimir |title=Sur les espaces localement connexes et péaniens en dimensions n |journal=Fundamenta Mathematicae |date=1935 |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=269–287 |url=https://eudml.org/doc/212754 |issn=0016-2736}}</ref><ref> Yukihiro Kodama. "On ''LC''<sup>n</sup> metric spaces." Proc. Japan Acad. 33 (2) 79 - 83, 1957. https://doi.org/10.3792/pja/1195525144</ref>

A topological space has the homotopy type of a countable CW-complex if and only if it has the homotopy type of an absolute neighborhood retract for separable metric spaces.<ref>Theorem 1 in {{cite journal | first = John | last = Milnor | author-link = John Milnor | title = On spaces having the homotopy type of CW-complex | journal = [[Transactions of the  American Mathematical Society]] | volume = 90 | number = 2 | year = 1959 | pages =  272–280 | doi = 10.2307/1993204 | jstor = 1993204}}</ref>

An open subset of a CW-complex may not be a CW-complex (due to Cauty). However, Cauty showed that a metric space is an ANR if and only if each open subset has the homotopy type of an ANR or equivalently the homtopy type of a CW-complex.<ref>Cauty, Robert (1994), "Une caractérisation des rétractes absolus de voisinage", Fundamenta Mathematicae, 144: 11–22, doi:10.4064/fm-144-1-11-22, MR 1271475.</ref>

== ANR homology manifold ==
{{expand section|date=December 2025}}
{{main|homology manifold}}

An '''ANR homology manifold''' of dimension ''n'' is a finite-dimensional ANR such that for each point <math>x</math> in <math>X</math>, the homology <math>\operatorname{H}_*(X, X - {x})</math> has <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> at ''n'' and zero elsewhere.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bryant |first1=J. |last2=Ferry |first2=S. |last3=Mio |first3=W. |last4=Weinberger |first4=S. |title=Topology of Homology Manifolds |journal=Annals of Mathematics |date=1996 |volume=143 |issue=3 |pages=435–467 |doi=10.2307/2118532 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2118532 |issn=0003-486X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
